Deconvolution with reference distributions: a review of methods that use more than the mean

Bastien Chassagnol

2026-10-28

Source: vignettes/theory-review-distribution-aware-deconvolution.qmd

Scope

First-generation deconvolution fits a bulk profile with the mean expression of each purified population. This review covers the methods that also use the distribution of the purified profiles: at least their variance, and in some cases a covariance between genes or between cell types. DeCovarT belongs to that family: it plugs in a gene–gene covariance per cell type and maximises a Gaussian-convolution likelihood (population generative vignette).

Every method is read through the same lens: what its observation law implies about the measurement process, most often UMI counts from single cells. Sec. 1 states the measurement and expression models that lens relies on, and Sec. 2.2 states the errors-in-variables problem that every method solves. The methods follow, grouped by what they estimate and what they assume known:

  1. reference-based estimation of the composition, split by whether genes are treated as independent (Sec. 2);
  2. cell-type-specific moments when the composition is known (Sec. 3);
  3. Bayesian reference-based methods, for profiles or for proportions (Sec. 4);
  4. semi-reference methods that infer one unknown component (Sec. 5);
  5. reference-free methods that use co-expression structure (Sec. 6).

Sec. 7 compares them and lists their caveats. The DeCovarT model rebuilt for single-cell references is in the single-cell generative vignette.

Note 1: Notation

Gene g=1,\ldots,G; cell type j=1,\ldots,J (a second type is \ell); bulk sample i=1,\ldots,N; reference donor (replicate) r=1,\ldots,R; cell c, with C_j cells of type j. Equations quoted from a paper are translated into these indices; only Table 2 keeps each paper’s own symbols.

Symbol Meaning
y_{gi}, \boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i} Bulk expression on a linear scale
m_{ji}, n_i=\sum_jm_{ji} Cells of type j in bulk sample i, and their total
\tilde{\boldsymbol{y}}_{\cdot i}=\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}/n_i Bulk expression per cell
\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}\in\Delta^{J-1} Cell-number fractions, p_{ji}=m_{ji}/n_i
\boldsymbol{q}_{\cdot i} Transcript fractions, q_{ji}=p_{ji}S_j/\sum_\ell p_{\ell i}S_\ell
\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}=C_j^{-1}\sum_{c\in j}\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot c}=S_j\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\cdot j} Per-cell mean of raw UMI counts of type j
\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\cdot j}, S_j=\mathbf{1}^{\top}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j} Relative abundance (\mathbf{1}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\cdot j}=1) and mean transcriptome size of a type-j cell
\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j Mean and G\times G gene–gene covariance of a type-j population profile (released DeCovarT)
\boldsymbol{\Omega}_j=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j^{-1} Precision of type j
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g J\times J covariance across cell types for gene g (bMIND, EPIC-unmix, Unico)
\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot j,i} Purified profile of type j in sample i
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{B,j} Within-type cell-to-cell covariance (per cell) and between-replicate covariance of type j
a_i Sample-wide scale
x_{gc}, s_c, \boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\cdot c} UMI count, size factor, size-free expression of cell c
b_g, \tilde b_g=b_g^{\mathrm{bulk}}/b_g^{\mathrm{ref}} Capture efficiency of one protocol, and the gene-wise platform ratio between bulk and reference; \tilde{\boldsymbol{B}}=\operatorname{diag}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{b}})

A tilde marks a quantity rescaled to a reference unit: per cell (\tilde{\boldsymbol{y}}, \tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}) or relative to the reference protocol (\tilde{\boldsymbol{b}}). Two kinds of covariance are kept apart throughout: \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j couples genes within one cell type; \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g couples cell types within one gene.

Measurement and expression models for single-cell counts

A reference profile is a moment of a latent biological quantity, but it is estimated from counts produced by a sampling protocol. Sarkar and Stephens separate the two: a measurement model p(\boldsymbol{x}\mid\boldsymbol{\lambda}) describes the protocol given the true expression, an expression model p(\boldsymbol{\lambda}) describes the biology, and the observation model p(\boldsymbol{x}) is their composition (Sarkar and Stephens 2021). Fang and Pachter add that the cell-level scale factor is itself a product of a biological and a technical term (Fang and Pachter 2025). Both papers index genes by j and cells by i; below, gene is g and cell is c, so that j remains the cell type.

Poisson measurement of UMI counts

If each molecule of cell c is captured independently with a small probability, the multivariate hypergeometric sampling of molecules is close to a multinomial and each gene count is Poisson given the true content (Supplementary Note 1 of (Sarkar and Stephens 2021)):

x_{gc}\mid s^{\mathrm{tech}}_c,m_{gc} \sim\mathrm{Poisson}\bigl(s^{\mathrm{tech}}_c\,b_g\,m_{gc}\bigr), \qquad \boldsymbol{m}_{\cdot c}=s^{\mathrm{bio}}_c\,\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\cdot c}. \tag{1}

Fang and Pachter write the same law as binomial thinning with capture rate b_gs^{\mathrm{tech}}_c, of which the Poisson is the low-capture limit, and normalise \mathbb{E}[s^{\mathrm{bio}}]=\mathbb{E}[s^{\mathrm{tech}}]=1 (their equations 1–2). Sarkar and Stephens instead take the observed library size x_{+c} as the size factor and a relative expression \lambda_{gc}=m_{gc}/m_{+c}; in that convention s^{\mathrm{bio}}_c cancels by construction, which is the removal of biological extrinsic noise that Fang and Pachter warn about. The two conventions are the two directions of the same rank-one Poisson fit: the point-mass MLE \hat\mu_g=\sum_cx_{gc}/\sum_cx_{+c} and the size-factor MLE of Eq. 3 below.

Three remarks connect the protocol to deconvolution.

  • UMIs remove most gene-specific distortion. Unique molecular identifiers collapse PCR duplicates, which “substantially reduce unwanted variation, including differences in gene lengths and PCR amplification efficiencies” (Sarkar and Stephens 2021). What remains is a capture efficiency b_g that is constant across cells of one protocol. It is not identified separately from \boldsymbol{\lambda}, and it cancels from every within-protocol contrast, so it is absorbed into \tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j} and \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}. It does not cancel between a single-cell reference and a bulk library: the ratio \tilde b_g=b_g^{\mathrm{bulk}}/b_g^{\mathrm{ref}} is the gene-wise platform factor of plug-in scales (Strategy 4). Read-count protocols without UMIs and hybridisation microarrays carry larger gene- and probe-specific factors (amplification, length, affinity), which is why earlier deconvolution methods had to model gene-wise scales explicitly; with UMI references, the gene-wise factor reduces to one cross-platform ratio per gene.
  • Random capture biases make the measurement overdispersed; constant ones do not. If b_{gc} varied from cell to cell, the measurement model would be negative binomial rather than Poisson (Box 1 and Supplementary Note 1.2 of Sarkar and Stephens). On spike-in controls the measurement dispersion was below 5\times10^{-3}, which adds about 5% to the variance of a gene with ten observed molecules. Overdispersion seen in single-cell data is therefore an expression property, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\lambda}_j, plus extrinsic noise, not a protocol property.
  • Zero inflation belongs to the expression model, if anywhere. Spike-in controls show no zero-generating measurement component, and a point-Gamma expression model beats a Gamma model for only 0.6–8.6% of genes across the datasets tested (Sarkar and Stephens 2021). Zeros are imperfect measurements of small \lambda_{gc} at low depth, “with no need for special terminology or special treatment”. For DeCovarT, which uses only the first two moments of the reference, a zero-inflated observation model is unnecessary: the moments of the counts already contain the zeros. The argument is made for UMI data; the authors note that it may not hold for read counts amplified by PCR without UMIs.

Expression models and the observation models they induce

Integrating the expression model against Eq. 1 gives the observation model gene by gene (Table 1 of (Sarkar and Stephens 2021)).

A gene whose expression model is a point mass inside a homogeneous population is a Poisson gene: its count has no variability beyond sampling and the extrinsic size factor. Overdispersion relative to a Poisson, the hallmark of the negative binomial, then measures either biological variability of \lambda_{gc} or variability of s_c.

Extrinsic noise, size factors and Poisson genes

Fang and Pachter show that a cell-wide factor explains the baseline overdispersion of single-cell counts. Under Eq. 1 with s_c=s^{\mathrm{bio}}_cs^{\mathrm{tech}}_c independent of \boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\cdot c}, \mathbb{E}[s_c]=1 and \nu=\operatorname{CV}^{2}(s_c), their equation (3) reads, in our notation and inside one cell type,

\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(x_{gc},x_{hc})}{\mathbb{E}[x_{gc}]\mathbb{E}[x_{hc}]} =\nu+(1+\nu)\frac{\Sigma^{\lambda}_{j,gh}}{\tilde\mu_{gj}\tilde\mu_{hj}} +\frac{\delta_{gh}}{\mathbb{E}[x_{gc}]}, \qquad 1+\nu=(1+\nu^{\mathrm{bio}})(1+\nu^{\mathrm{tech}}). \tag{2}

For two genes that are intrinsically uncorrelated, or for one gene that is intrinsically Poisson, the normalised covariance equals \nu (their equation 5). That identity gives an estimator of \nu (the mode of the normalised covariances over gene pairs) and a selection rule for Poisson genes (those whose normalised variance minus the Poisson term has a bootstrap interval containing \hat\nu). On those genes \mathcal{P}, the size factor has the closed-form MLE

\hat s_c=\frac{\sum_{g\in\mathcal{P}}x_{gc}}{\sum_{g\in\mathcal{P}}\tilde\mu_{gj}}. \tag{3}

Two findings matter here. Normalising each cell by its total removes s^{\mathrm{bio}}_c together with s^{\mathrm{tech}}_c, and with it the biological extrinsic variability, including cell size (Fang and Pachter 2025). In peripheral blood, sums over Poisson genes no longer track total UMI counts and differ between cell types, so the choice of size factor changes downstream comparisons. Separating s^{\mathrm{tech}}_c from s^{\mathrm{bio}}_c needs external controls (spike-ins, ambient RNA, pooled RNA); the nascent-mRNA counts did not fit the binomial sampling model in their pooled-RNA experiment.

What the measurement model implies for the reference covariance

Write the same identity in matrix form (a direct consequence of Eq. 1 and the law of total covariance; the derivation is ours). With \boldsymbol{\mathcal{B}}=\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol{b}),

\operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot c}\mid c\in j) =\underbrace{\operatorname{diag}\bigl(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{B}}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}\bigr)}_{\text{Poisson measurement}} +\boldsymbol{\mathcal{B}}\Bigl[ \underbrace{(1+\nu)\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\lambda}_j}_{\text{biology}} +\underbrace{\nu\,\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}^{\top}}_{\text{size factor}} \Bigr]\boldsymbol{\mathcal{B}}. \tag{4}

The sample covariance of raw UMI counts, which is what a single-cell reference returns as \hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{W,j}, mixes three objects. Only part of it belongs in the bulk law.

  1. The Poisson diagonal is single-cell measurement noise. It is produced at single-cell depth and is not part of the tissue. A bulk library has its own sampling noise, on its own depth, which a diagonal bulk term would carry. Plugging raw-count covariances into \boldsymbol{S}_W imports the reference sampling noise into the bulk covariance; subtracting \operatorname{diag}(\bar{\boldsymbol{x}}_j) first removes it.
  2. The technical size-factor term is not biology either. The rank-one term \nu^{\mathrm{tech}}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}^{\top} induces a positive correlation between all genes. It inflates the apparent network and is a protocol artefact.
  3. The biological size factor is part of the bulk. Cells of one type differ in volume and cycle phase; a tissue sums those cells as they are. The term \nu^{\mathrm{bio}}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}^{\top} belongs in \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}, and library-size normalisation that removes it understates the within-type variance that the bulk accumulates.

The corresponding moment estimator, with \hat\nu^{\mathrm{tech}} from spike-ins or Poisson genes, is

\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{W,j} =\hat{\boldsymbol{C}}_j-\operatorname{diag}(\bar{\boldsymbol{x}}_j) -\frac{\hat\nu^{\mathrm{tech}}}{1+\hat\nu^{\mathrm{tech}}}\, \bigl[\hat{\boldsymbol{C}}_j-\operatorname{diag}(\bar{\boldsymbol{x}}_j)+\bar{\boldsymbol{x}}_j\bar{\boldsymbol{x}}_j^{\top}\bigr], \tag{5}

where \hat{\boldsymbol{C}}_j is the sample covariance of the type-j counts and \bar{\boldsymbol{x}}_j their mean. It is the s^{\mathrm{tech}}-free covariance of \boldsymbol{\mathcal{B}}\boldsymbol{m}_{\cdot c} obtained by solving Eq. 4 with 1+\nu=(1+\nu^{\mathrm{bio}})(1+\nu^{\mathrm{tech}}) (our derivation, to be checked by simulation before use). Estimating \nu^{\mathrm{tech}} before the deconvolution is the first plug-in of Strategy 4 (plug-in scales (Strategy 4)).

Before single cells: measurement models for sorted population profiles

Before droplet single-cell sequencing, a reference column was a bulk measurement of a physically sorted population: FACS or magnetic sorting, then a microarray or a bulk RNA-seq library. The measurement model was the one of the platform, applied to a pool of many cells.

  • Microarrays. A probe intensity is a background plus a probe-specific affinity times the abundance, with errors that are roughly additive at low intensity and multiplicative at high intensity. Analyses of differential expression worked on \log_2 intensities, where the multiplicative error becomes additive. Deconvolution could not: mixing is additive in the abundance, so the first reference-based methods fitted linear models on unlogged intensities (Abbas et al. 2009; Shen-Orr et al. 2010; Lähdesmäki et al. 2005). The probe affinity is a gene-wise factor of the platform. It cancels within one platform and does not cancel between platforms, which is the origin of the gene-wise platform ratio \tilde{\boldsymbol{b}} of later methods.
  • Bulk RNA-seq of sorted populations. Reads are counts with a library size and a gene-length factor (for full-length protocols). Replicate libraries of one sorted population vary by a negative binomial dispersion that mixes biological and technical variation. Normalised counts on a linear scale (CPM, TPM) became the default input, with the same warning against logarithms.
  • What the reference variance meant. With a handful of sorted replicates per population, the only second-order quantity available was a between-replicate variance of the population mean. That is the quadratic layer \sum_jp_j^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{B,j} of the single-cell generative vignette, and the object released DeCovarT was designed for. A within-type, cell-to-cell covariance did not exist in that design.

Two biases of sorted references have no single-cell analogue: sorting selects cells on a few surface markers, so a “pure” population can contain contaminating types; and the sorting itself can change expression before lysis. Single-cell references remove the first by labelling cells after the fact, and replace the platform model by the Poisson measurement of Sec. 1.1.

From measurement models to bulk observation laws

A deconvolution method chooses a law for the bulk. Read with the split of Sec. 1, that law is a measurement model (multinomial, Poisson) composed with an expression model for the purified profiles (Gaussian, log-normal, Gamma). Figure 3 places the methods of this review by the support of \boldsymbol{y} first.

Discrete counts

A multinomial (or Dirichlet–multinomial) model treats \boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i} as integer reads that sum to a library size. ISOpureR implements a hierarchical multinomial–Dirichlet purification of mixed tumour profiles (Anghel et al. 2015). BayesPrism places a multinomial likelihood on bulk counts with a patient-derived scRNA-seq prior and jointly infers \boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i} and sample-level CTS expression (Chu et al. 2022). DeconV instead uses Poisson aggregation from single-cell to bulk (sums of independent Poissons remain Poisson) and returns interval estimates of \boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i} (Gynter et al. 2023). RCTD is a Poisson–log-normal mixture of reads (Sec. 2.3.6).

Over-dispersed, correlated counts are the domain of the multivariate Poisson–log-normal (PLN) family: a latent Gaussian vector induces dependence, and a Poisson observation layer yields integer reads (Chiquet et al. 2021, 2018). ZIPLN adds a Bernoulli zero-inflation layer for dropout (Batardière et al. 2025). A DeCovarT-style extension would replace Eq. 18 by a PLN (or ZIPLN) convolution on the latent log-abundance scale, keeping the ILR chart on \boldsymbol{p}. A multinomial logit-normal on the gene simplex is a different discrete model: it is compositional association, not a cell-type convolution (two simplices without convolution).

Second-generation deconvolution: univariate versus multivariate

Second-generation methods use a single-cell reference and model, in some form, the variability of the cell-type profiles. The usual split into regression and probabilistic engines hides the property that matters for DeCovarT: whether the bulk model treats genes as independent (a diagonal variance per gene) or keeps a gene–gene covariance. Figure 4 uses that split.

A common notation

Each paper uses its own indices; several use j for the gene or the subject. Table 2 maps them to this vignette. The scale columns show how one model is reparametrised into another by arithmetic alone.

Three reparametrisations recur.

  • Counts to fractions. A model in cell counts, \boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}=\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\boldsymbol{m}_{\cdot i}, becomes a model in fractions after division by the number of cells, \tilde{\boldsymbol{y}}_{\cdot i}=\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}. RNA-Sieve keeps n_i as a parameter; DWLS estimates \boldsymbol{m}_{\cdot i} (its “cell-type numbers”) and normalises at the end.
  • Total molecules to average cell size. MuSiC equation (2) gives \sum_gX_{gi}=n_i\sum_jp_{ji}S_j. Dividing by n_i gives the average cell size of the sample, \bar S_i=\sum_jp_{ji}S_j, and MuSiC’s normalising constant is its inverse, C_i=\bar S_i^{-1}. Library-size normalisation therefore returns transcript fractions q_{ji}=p_{ji}S_j/\bar S_i, not cell fractions.
  • Scale times composition. MEAD estimates \boldsymbol{\beta}_i=a_i\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i} and RCTD p_{ji}e^{\alpha_i}; both normalise at the end. The total of the unnormalised weights identifies the sample scale (the sample-wide capture scale).

The common problem: errors in variables

Every method of this review estimates a composition from two noisy views of one latent truth: the purified profile \boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot j,i} of each type in each sample. The bulk mixes these profiles; the reference supplies only an estimate of their mean:

\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}=\sum_jp_{ji}\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot j,i}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_i, \qquad \boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot j,i}=\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j}+\boldsymbol{u}_{\cdot j,i}, \qquad \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}=\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j}+\boldsymbol{v}_{\cdot j}, \tag{6}

with three mean-zero errors: the biological deviation \boldsymbol{u}_{\cdot j,i} of sample i from the type mean, the measurement noise \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_i of the bulk library, and the estimation error \boldsymbol{v}_{\cdot j} of a reference built from finitely many cells or donors. Substituting the reference gives the regression that every method fits, \boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}=\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}+\boldsymbol{e}_i with \boldsymbol{e}_i=\sum_jp_{ji}(\boldsymbol{u}_{\cdot j,i}-\boldsymbol{v}_{\cdot j})+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_i: an errors-in-variables model whose regressor is the reference. The methods differ by two choices.

  • Where the error is modelled. \boldsymbol{v} is an error in the regressor, the classical errors-in-variables layer; ignoring it biases \hat{\boldsymbol{p}} (attenuation, in the linear case) and understates its variance. RNA-Sieve models it in a joint likelihood and MEAD removes it with a bias-corrected estimating equation; every other method plugs \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}} in as exact and models the response error \sum_jp_{ji}\boldsymbol{u}_{\cdot j,i}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_i only.
  • How the error is specified. (a) By a parametric law: Gaussian in DeCovarT, Poisson–log-normal in RCTD, Poisson in DeconV.
    1. By an asymptotic law: the central limit over the n_i cells of a sample, gene by gene, in RNA-Sieve and ReDeconv; the central limit over genes, G\to\infty, in MEAD and DECALS. (c) By its first two conditional moments only, \mathbb{E}(\boldsymbol{e}_i\mid\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i})=\boldsymbol{0} and a working \operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol{e}_i\mid\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}), the route by which ordinary least squares is justified without a Gaussian assumption (Agresti 2015, ch. 2). DECALS states this choice; MuSiC, DWLS and deMixSC make it implicitly through their gene weights.

The textbook assumptions do not hold here. The classical model takes the errors independent of the true regressor and of each other, with a constant variance (terminology and assumptions). In DeCovarT the response error has covariance \sum_jp_{ji}^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j, a function of the parameter; in Poisson models (RCTD, DeconV) the variance equals the mean, again a function of \boldsymbol{p}. Our reading: once the type mean is assigned and the sample profile scatters around it independently of that mean, the \boldsymbol{u} layer is a Berkson error, which does not bias a linear estimator but enters weighted by the coefficients p_{ji}, hence heteroscedastically. The \boldsymbol{v} layer is classical, and DeCovarT ignores it by plugging in \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}, which is defensible only when every type has many reference cells.

Moment estimators give point estimates. Weighted non-negative least squares (MuSiC, DWLS, deMixSC) solves the normal equations \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{\top}\boldsymbol{W}(\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}-\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i})=\boldsymbol{0}, and Unico matches first and second sample moments explicitly. All are generalised method of moments estimators: consistent under correct moment conditions, but they return a point estimate only. An interval needs more: a variance model with a sandwich (DECALS), a likelihood (RNA-Sieve, DeCovarT) or a resampling unit (genes, cells or donors). When the weights are re-estimated from the residuals of the same fit (MuSiC, deMixSC), the nominal weighted-least-squares covariance is not valid either (our remark).

Univariate methods: genes independent

MuSiC

MuSiC starts from molecules: the bulk of subject i holds X_{gi}=\sum_jm_{ji}S_j\theta_{gj}=\sum_jm_{ji}\tilde\mu_{gj}, with S_j the mean total molecules per cell of type j (equation 2). It works on relative abundance Y_{gi}=X_{gi}/\sum_{g'}X_{g'i}, so that, with the reparametrisation above,

Y_{gi}=C_i\Bigl(\sum_jp_{ji}S_j\theta_{gj}+\varepsilon_{gi}\Bigr), \qquad \operatorname{Var}(Y_{gi}\mid\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}) =C_i^{2}\delta_{gi}^{2}+C_i^{2}\sum_jp_{ji}^{2}S_j^{2}\sigma^{2}_{gj} =w_{gi}^{-1} \tag{7}

(equations 8–10). The second term comes from subject-level relative profiles \theta_{gj,i}\sim F(\theta_{gj},\sigma^{2}_{gj}) (assumption A1): it is the diagonal of the between-replicate layer \boldsymbol{S}_B(\boldsymbol{p}), quadratic in p_{ji}, and it requires a multi-subject reference. Cross terms between types are dropped, which implicitly assumes independence across types. \delta^{2}_{gi} is the residual variance of the bulk. The within-type cell scatter \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j} has no term in Eq. 7; it is used only to select genes with small within-cluster variance in the tree-guided recursion. Estimation is weighted non-negative least squares, with the weights updated from an initial fit because \delta^{2}_{gi} is unknown, followed by rescaling to the simplex.

Scales and identifiability. S_j is plugged in as the mean library size of type j in the reference. That substitution returns cell fractions only under assumption A3', a capture efficiency (observed library size over molecule content) common to all types (the MuSiC assumptions); otherwise MuSiC estimates the RNA-weighted product p_{ji}S_j. Under A1–A3 alone the paper claims only the trend of proportions across subjects. Absolute S_j is not needed: it cancels into C_i. A gene- and subject-specific intercept \alpha_{gi} absorbs protocol bias. MuSiC2 keeps the weights and removes genes that are differentially expressed between the reference and bulk conditions (Fan et al. 2022).

Errors in variables (Sec. 2.2): response error only, specified by two moments with a diagonal variance; \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}} is plugged in, and the estimator is a weighted moment estimator.

RNA-Sieve

RNA-Sieve writes the bulk as a sum of n cells, each a draw from the cell mixture the mixture-of-cells covariance restricted to one gene. By the central limit theorem,

y_{gi}\sim\mathcal{N}\bigl(n_i(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i})_g,\ n_i\sigma^{2}_{gi}\bigr), \qquad \sigma^{2}_{gi}=\sum_jp_{ji}\bigl(V_{gj}+\tilde\mu_{gj}^{2}\bigr)-(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i})_g^{2}, \tag{8}

with genes independent (equations 5–8). The variance is linear in n_i and in \boldsymbol{p}, minus the square of the mixture mean: the within-type variance \sum_jp_{ji}V_{gj} plus the spread of the type means, the diagonal of the mixture-of-cells covariance. The reference means are noisy, \hat{\tilde\mu}_{gj}\sim\mathcal{N}(\tilde\mu_{gj},V_{gj}/C_j) (equation 9), and the true means are estimated jointly with (\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i},n_i) from all bulks (equations 10–11). Marginalising them instead would add n_i^{2}\sum_jp_{ji}^{2}V_{gj}/C_j to the variance, a quadratic term that vanishes as the reference grows (our remark).

Scales. Raw counts keep S_j inside \mathbf{M}, so \boldsymbol{\alpha} are cell fractions; the optional rescaling of every cell to the median library size removes S_j and turns them into RNA fractions. Any global protocol difference is absorbed into n_i, which then “loses interpretability” as a cell number across protocols (Supplementary S1.4). Intervals come from the observed Fisher information or, by default, from the Godambe matrix, centred at the Kullback–Leibler projection under misspecification. The paper notes that gene correlation “may be incorporated” once it is known, but does not implement it.

Errors in variables (Sec. 2.2): both layers; the response error has an asymptotic (central-limit) law over cells, and the regressor error is modelled in a joint likelihood.

DWLS

DWLS fits the cell-type numbers \mathbf{x}=\boldsymbol{m}_{\cdot i} by

\hat{\boldsymbol{m}}_{\cdot i} =\arg\min_{\boldsymbol{m}\ge\boldsymbol{0}}\sum_g\bar w_{gi}\bigl(y_{gi}-\hat{\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}_{g\cdot}\boldsymbol{m}\bigr)^{2}, \qquad \bar w_{gi}=\min\Bigl\{w_{\max},\ \frac{(\hat{\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}_{g\cdot}\hat{\boldsymbol{m}}_{\cdot i})^{-2}}{\min_{g'}(\hat{\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}_{g'\cdot}\hat{\boldsymbol{m}}_{\cdot i})^{-2}}\Bigr\}, \tag{9}

iterated from an ordinary least squares start, with w_{\max}=2^{q} chosen to minimise the variance of estimates over random half-gene subsets (equations 6–15). The purpose is stated on p. 7: with weights 1/(\text{fitted expression})^{2} the loss becomes a function of the relative error of each cell type, “because we would like all cell types to be estimated with equal accuracy”; highly expressed genes, which dominate an unweighted fit and favour abundant types, are down-weighted. Read as a variance model, the weights imply \operatorname{Var}(y_{gi})\propto(\hat{\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}_{g\cdot}\boldsymbol{m}_{\cdot i})^{2}, a constant coefficient of variation, which the paper does not state. There is no \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j} term and genes are independent. \mathbf{x} are cell numbers only under equal RNA per cell; otherwise they are RNA-weighted.

Errors in variables (Sec. 2.2): response error only, two moments with a variance proportional to the squared mean; a weighted moment estimator with no interval.

deMixSC

deMixSC keeps the weighted non-negative least squares of MuSiC and DWLS and adds a small benchmark data set: bulk and single-nucleus libraries prepared from the same nucleus aliquot, so that the real bulk and the pseudo-bulk share the composition (Guo et al. 2025, p. 149). In the 24 benchmark retinas, more than 5000 genes differ between the two platforms in each batch, and TPM normalisation does not remove the difference. In our notation the working model is (supplementary note, equations S.1–S.5, pp. 1–2)

y_{gi}=n_i\sum_jp_{ji}\tilde\mu_{gj}+\epsilon_{gi}, \qquad \tilde\mu_{gj}=S_j\theta_{gj}, \qquad \hat{\tilde\mu}_{gj}=\tilde\mu_{gj}+\bar\xi_{gj}, \tag{10}

with mean-zero bulk noise \epsilon_{gi} and an averaged single-cell measurement error \bar\xi_{gj}. The residual of a fit with \hat{\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}} is the estimation error plus a “technological discrepancy” between platforms (note, p. 3). Two changes to weighted NNLS follow.

  • Partitioned loss (equation S.7, note p. 3). Genes differentially expressed between real bulk and pseudo-bulk in the benchmark form a set G_2 (5000 genes by default); their bulk value and reference are divided by a constant a (1000 by default), which scales their squared residuals by a^{-2}:

    \hat{\boldsymbol{p}}_{\cdot i}=\arg\min_{\boldsymbol{p}\ge\boldsymbol{0}} \sum_{g\in G_1}w_{gi}\,r_{gi}(\boldsymbol{p})^{2} +\frac{1}{a^{2}}\sum_{g\in G_2}w_{gi}\,r_{gi}(\boldsymbol{p})^{2}, \qquad r_{gi}(\boldsymbol{p})=y_{gi}-n_i\sum_jp_{ji}\hat{\tilde\mu}_{gj}. \tag{11}

  • Weights (equation S.9, note p. 3; main text p. 150): w_{gi}^{-1}=\hat y_{gi}^{2}+(y_{gi}-\hat y_{gi})^{2}+c, with \hat y_{gi}=n_i\sum_j\hat p_{ji}\hat{\tilde\mu}_{gj} and c=2. Earlier methods, the authors note, use “either the squared fitted value” (DWLS, Eq. 9) “or the variance” (MuSiC’s iteratively estimated \delta^{2}_{gi}, Eq. 7), “but never both” (p. 157). The fit is iterated from an NNLS start (note, p. 4).

The target cohort is first aligned to the benchmark bulk by quantile normalisation and ComBat (p. 150). The platform effect is treated as noise to down-weight, not as a gene-wise ratio \tilde b_g to estimate: with a=1000 the genes of G_2 receive a weight 10^{-6} times smaller, which nearly discards them. The squared residual in the weight uses one residual per gene as its own variance, an outlier-damping device in the spirit of robust M-estimation rather than a variance model (our reading). Cell size enters through \tilde\mu_{gj}=S_j\theta_{gj}, as in MuSiC, so \hat{\boldsymbol{p}} are cell fractions under the same equal-efficiency assumption. No interval is reported.

Errors in variables (Sec. 2.2): both layers are written down but enter only through the weights; a weighted moment estimator with no interval.

Bisque

Bisque learns the platform shift instead of modelling it. In paired mode it fits y^{\mathrm{ps}}_{gi'}=\beta_{0g}+\beta_gy_{gi'}+\epsilon_{gi'} per gene, with \boldsymbol{y}^{\mathrm{ps}}_{\cdot i'}=\boldsymbol{\theta}\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i'} the pseudo-bulk of individual i' (equation 1); in unpaired mode it matches the first two moments of each gene across samples (equations 2–3). The transformed bulk is then fitted by non-negative least squares with a sum-to-one constraint. The fitting step has homoscedastic residuals; the variability of the reference enters only through the between-sample moments used in the map. Because \boldsymbol{\theta} is built from CPM, cell size is removed from the signature; the gene-wise affine map absorbs the platform ratio \tilde b_g (as 1/\beta_g) and an intercept, not a type-specific S_j. In unpaired mode the cohort mean composition is assumed equal to the mean composition of the single-cell individuals.

Errors in variables (Sec. 2.2): the platform error is removed by a learned map, then a homoscedastic moment estimator; no interval.

RCTD

RCTD works one layer below DeCovarT. Each UMI first picks a type with probability p_{ji}, then a gene from that type’s relative profile: a read-level mixture, not a convolution of random population profiles (Cable et al. 2022). Given the rate, gene counts are Poisson; the rate is log-normal around a linear mixture of the fixed normalised means \theta_{gj} (supplementary equations 3, 22):

y_{gi}\mid\lambda_{gi}\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(L_i\lambda_{gi}), \qquad \log\lambda_{gi}=\alpha_i+\log\Bigl(\sum_jp_{ji}\theta_{gj}\Bigr)+\gamma_g+\varepsilon_{gi}, \tag{12}

with L_i the observed depth, \alpha_i a leftover sample scale, \gamma_g the platform effect and \varepsilon_{gi} an independent, heavy-tailed \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_\varepsilon^2) overdispersion. The Poisson mean is

\mathbb{E}[y_{gi}\mid\varepsilon_{gi}] =\underbrace{L_ie^{\alpha_i}}_{a_i}\,\tilde b_g\,e^{\varepsilon_{gi}}\sum_jp_{ji}\theta_{gj}, \qquad \tilde b_g=e^{\gamma_g}, \tag{13}

so the platform effect is exactly the gene-wise ratio \tilde b_g of Sec. 1.1, and \varepsilon_{gi} is the count-scale analogue of a diagonal bulk residual. Genes are independent given \varepsilon. In the language of the measurement model, the rate of gene g is a type-weighted sum of per-type rates scaled by one sample-wide factor; the same holds in DeCovarT’s single-cell mean a_in_i\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}, whose per-type contribution is n_ip_{ji}S_j molecules of profile \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\cdot j} (our reading). A mixture is the right story at the UMI; a convolution of random profiles (Eq. 18) is the right story for population profiles.

The fit is two-stage because \tilde{\boldsymbol{b}} cannot be free inside one sample (alignment scales): stage 1 estimates \gamma_g from one pseudobulk of all spots (supplementary equations 14–19), stage 2 holds it fixed. That is Strategy 4 in its purest form (plug-in scales). Stage 2 maximises a non-convex Poisson–log-normal likelihood in w_{ji}=p_{ji}e^{\alpha_i}\ge0 by sequential quadratic programming: the Hessian is replaced by its positive-semidefinite part and each step is a constrained quadratic programme with step size 0.3. Zeros on the orthant boundary are native to that formulation, which suits spots with few types. DeCovarT instead maps \boldsymbol{p} to the ILR chart and takes Newton–Raphson steps with the analytic score and Hessian of a Gaussian law.

Errors in variables (Sec. 2.2): response error only, with a parametric (Poisson–log-normal) law; the reference means are plugged in and the platform ratio is a plug-in from stage 1.

ReDeconv

ReDeconv names three ways a single-cell reference distorts deconvolution: rescaling every cell to a common total (CP10K), which erases transcriptome size; the gene-length mismatch between UMI single-cell counts and full-length bulk libraries; and ignoring the within-type variance (Lu et al. 2025).

Model. The bulk is a sum of m_{ji} independent cells of each type. By the central limit theorem, after a rescaling of the bulk by a constant c and with weights f_{ji}=cm_{ji},

y_{gi}\sim\mathcal{N}\Bigl(\sum_jf_{ji}\tilde\mu_{gj},\ c\sum_jf_{ji}\sigma^{2}_{gj}\Bigr), \tag{14}

with genes independent, and the composition is estimated by maximising the product of these densities over genes. The variance is linear in the weights, the diagonal of the within-type layer n_i^{-1}\sum_jp_{ji}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j} (one replicate), as in RNA-Sieve without the spread of type means. The optimiser, the estimation of c and the final simplex step are not stated.

Transcriptome size. CLTS normalisation fits, for each single-cell sample r, a line S_{jr}=\alpha_rS_{j1}+\beta_r between its mean transcriptome sizes per type and those of a baseline sample, then rescales every count of sample r as x_{gc}\leftarrow x_{gc}/\alpha_r+(v_{\max}-\beta_r/\alpha_r)/G with v_{\max}=\max_r\beta_r/\alpha_r. Differences of transcriptome size between types within a sample are kept; differences between samples are removed. CLTS therefore keeps S_j in \tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}=S_j\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\cdot j}, so the fitted weights are cell fractions rather than transcript fractions.

Caveats. About 100 signature genes per type are chosen by a t-test, a fold change and a small coefficient of variation; the synthetic benchmarks draw bulk and reference from the same single-cell source, as the authors acknowledge.

Errors in variables (Sec. 2.2): response error only, with an asymptotic (central-limit) law over cells; the reference is plugged in.

Multivariate methods: gene–gene covariance

DECALS

DECALS makes no distributional assumption on the bulk. Its model (equations 1–2, 5) is

\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}=\sum_jp_{ji}\boldsymbol{x}^{(j)}_i =\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_i, \qquad \operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_i)=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i=\sum_jp_{ji}^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j, \tag{15}

with subject-level type profiles \boldsymbol{x}^{(j)}_i independent across types: exactly the quadratic layer \boldsymbol{S}_B(\boldsymbol{p}) and released DeCovarT’s covariance, without a density. The three panels of Figure 11 are the paper’s three estimators.

  1. Constrained OLS (equation 3) is the point estimator. For a large number of genes the inequality constraints are inactive and the estimator is the equality-constrained projection \hat{\boldsymbol{p}}=\mathbf{U}\tilde{\boldsymbol{p}} of the OLS solution (Lemma S1). Its asymptotic covariance is the sandwich \boldsymbol{V}_i=\mathbf{U}\mathbf{D}\mathbf{U}^{\top} with \mathbf{D}=(\tfrac1G\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\mu})^{-1}\tfrac1G\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i\boldsymbol{\mu}(\tfrac1G\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\mu})^{-1}.
  2. Constrained GLS with known \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i (equations 10–11) is more efficient. The authors reject it once \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i is estimated: the per-sample inverse square root is too noisy, and the coverage of GLS with an estimated covariance falls to about 0.65–0.8 in their simulations.
  3. Unknown \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j. Because \mathbb{E}[z_{gi}z_{hi}]=\sum_jp_{ji}^{2}\Sigma_{j,gh}, the residual outer products are regressed on the squared proportions across the N samples, \hat{\boldsymbol{c}}_{gh}=(\hat{\mathbf{H}}^{\top}\hat{\mathbf{H}})^{-1}\hat{\mathbf{H}}^{\top}(\hat{\boldsymbol{z}}_g\circ\hat{\boldsymbol{z}}_h) with \hat{\mathbf{H}}=[\hat p_{ji}^{2}] (equation 6), a regression first proposed for known proportions by CSNet. Replacing \mathbf{H} by \hat{\mathbf{H}} deflates the estimate; Proposition 1 gives the bias terms \mathbf{B}_1,\mathbf{B}_2 under a Gaussian approximation of \hat{\boldsymbol{p}}, and the corrected estimator (equation 7) is iterated with \boldsymbol{V}_i, then thresholded by SCAD and projected onto the positive semidefinite cone.

Asymptotics. Genes are the statistical units: Theorem 1 gives \sqrt{G}(\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}_{\cdot i}-\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i})\to\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\boldsymbol{V}_i) as G\to\infty for one sample, under sub-exponential errors, a dependency graph of bounded degree among genes, and p_{ji}>0 for all types. On a face of the simplex the limit law is not derived. With dense gene correlation the authors report that coverage collapses to about 0.65: the central limit theorem over genes fails when dependence is not sparse. The paper gives no consistency theorem for \hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_j.

Errors in variables (Sec. 2.2): response error only, specified by two moments with the composition-dependent covariance of DeCovarT; an asymptotic law over genes yields the sandwich interval.

MEAD

MEAD is the multivariate errors-in-variables method. Its successive models (Figure 12), translated into our indices, are:

  • Scales (equations 2–3). The bulk is \boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}=a_i\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol{b}^{\mathrm{bulk}})\mathbf{X}_i\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_i and reference individual r is \mathbf{Z}_r=a^{\mathrm{ref}}_r\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol{b}^{\mathrm{ref}})\mathbf{X}^{\mathrm{ref}}_r+\mathbf{E}_r, with \mathbf{X}_i and \mathbf{X}^{\mathrm{ref}}_r drawn from one population law (assumption 1). a_i captures depth and tissue amount, \boldsymbol{b} gene length and GC content. The reference scale is one scalar per reference individual, shared by its cell types (Supplementary S2.1); the authors avoid per-cell library-size normalisation to keep cell size in \boldsymbol{\mu}.

  • Reparametrisation (equations 4–5). Only the ratio \tilde b_g=b^{\mathrm{bulk}}_g/b^{\mathrm{ref}}_g is identified, and assumption 3 treats it as noise, \tilde b_g\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}[1,\sigma_0^{2}], independent of \boldsymbol{\mu}. The model becomes \boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}=\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{\beta}_i+\boldsymbol{e}_i with \boldsymbol{\beta}_i=a_i\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i} and \boldsymbol{e}_i=(\tilde{\boldsymbol{B}}-\mathbf{I})\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{\beta}_i+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}'_i: the platform ratio is not estimated, inflates the variance and makes \boldsymbol{e}_i dependent across samples.

  • One sample. With \hat a^{\mathrm{ref}}_r=\sum_{j,g}z_{rgj}/(JG) (a plug-in from the reference alone), \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{g\cdot} the average of \boldsymbol{z}_{rg\cdot}/\hat a^{\mathrm{ref}}_r and \hat{\mathbf{V}}_g its covariance across reference individuals, the bias-corrected estimating equation

    \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{\top}\mathbf{W}\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}-\bigl(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{\top}\mathbf{W}\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}-\hat{\mathbf{V}}\bigr)\boldsymbol{\beta}_i=\boldsymbol{0}, \qquad \hat{\mathbf{V}}=\sum_gw_g\hat{\mathbf{V}}_g, \tag{16}

    removes the attenuation caused by a noisy regressor (equation 6). Non-negativity is imposed by truncation or constrained optimisation, and \hat{\boldsymbol{p}}_{\cdot i}=\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_i/\|\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_i\|_1.

  • Several samples (section 5). The composition is regressed on covariates, \mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}]=h(\boldsymbol{b}_0+\mathbf{A}_0^{\top}\boldsymbol{f}_i), with \hat{\boldsymbol{p}}_{\cdot i} plugged into an estimating equation (11).

  • Dependence and weights. Gene–gene dependence is global, not type specific: a dependency graph over genes, estimated from the bulk correlation by a multiple test, enters only the sandwich covariance. The weights w_g=1/\tilde s_g^{2}, with s_g^{2}=\mathbf{1}^{\top}\hat{\mathbf{V}}_g\mathbf{1} shrunk across genes, come from the reference only; MuSiC’s residual-based weights “can severely bias” the estimating equation.

Identifiability (Theorem 1). With a composition matrix of rank J, the proportions are identifiable if and only if \boldsymbol{\mu} has full rank and, for every partition of the genes into t\ge2 blocks, the ranks of the blocks of \boldsymbol{\mu} add to more than J. Perfect marker genes violate the condition: rescaling the platform ratios of the type-j markers by 1/\delta_j, the proportions to \tilde p_{ji}=\delta_jp_{ji}/\sum_\ell\delta_\ell p_{\ell i} and the scale to a_i\sum_\ell\delta_\ell p_{\ell i} leaves the bulk mean unchanged, for any \boldsymbol{\delta}. A gene-wise platform ratio can then mimic a type-specific size factor (Supplementary Remark S1), the \boldsymbol{q} versus \boldsymbol{p} ambiguity of alignment scales; assumption 3 restores identification because a ratio that depends on the type of its marker is no longer independent of \boldsymbol{\mu} (our reading).

Asymptotics. With G\to\infty and the number of reference individuals fixed, Theorems 2–3 give \sqrt{G}(\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}_{\cdot i}-\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i})\to\mathcal{N}\bigl(\boldsymbol{0},\nabla g\,\boldsymbol{\Upsilon}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i\boldsymbol{\Upsilon}^{-1}\nabla g^{\top}\bigr), with the Gram limit \boldsymbol{\Upsilon}=\lim G^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\top}\mathbf{W}\boldsymbol{\mu}, when every p_{ji}>0 and the dependency graph is “almost sparse”. The regime is fragile when the reference-noise term does not shrink (fixed number of reference individuals), when types are collinear, at the boundary (the softplus device is inconsistent for finite tuning), and for the composition regression unless N=o(G) (Theorem 4, Remark S3). DECALS reports that MEAD underestimates variances.

Errors in variables (Sec. 2.2): both layers; the regressor error is removed by a bias-corrected estimating equation and the platform ratio is a multiplicative response error; the law is asymptotic in G.

Where DeCovarT sits

Released DeCovarT plugs in the mean and gene–gene covariance of each type and fits the Gaussian convolution of Eq. 18, one bulk sample at a time. Against the methods above:

  • RNA-Sieve and ReDeconv sum independent cells, so a type’s variance enters linearly in p_{ji}, gene by gene; DeCovarT convolves random population profiles, so it enters quadratically and keeps the gene–gene covariance.
  • DECALS assumes the same covariance, \sum_jp_{ji}^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j, without a density; its point estimate is least squares and its efficiency depends on how well the covariance is estimated across bulks. MEAD keeps a global gene dependence and adds the platform ratio, but models the reference noise that DeCovarT ignores.
  • RCTD is a read-level mixture with gene-wise overdispersion, not a type-level covariance.

For a single-cell reference the bulk is a physical sum of cells, and the variance becomes linear in p_{ji}, as in RNA-Sieve. The strategies that rebuild DeCovarT for that reference, and the three-layer law that combines within- and between-donor covariances, are in the single-cell generative vignette; the model retained for real data is in the MLE vignette.

Cell-type-specific moments when the composition is known

The methods of Sec. 2 estimate the composition from known reference moments. The reverse problem takes the composition \{\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}\} as known, from any of those methods, and estimates what DeCovarT plugs in: type-level means and covariances, or the purified profile of each type in each sample. Write the convolution with explicit latent profiles,

\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot j,i}\sim(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j)\ \text{independent across }j, \qquad \boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}=\sum_jp_{ji}\,\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot j,i}, \tag{17}

so that

\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}]=\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}, \qquad \operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i})=\sum_jp_{ji}^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j , \tag{18}

which is the released DeCovarT law when the profiles are Gaussian. Three families use these identities.

  • Type-level gene networks across a cohort. CSNet regresses the outer products of bulk residuals on the squared proportions to estimate each \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j, then thresholds the correlation (Sec. 3.1).
  • Sample-level profiles with a covariance across cell types. Unico (Sec. 3.2), and the Bayesian bMIND and EPIC-unmix (Sec. 4.1), place a J\times J covariance \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g across cell types for each gene, independent across genes. Their covariance is the transpose of DeCovarT’s: it couples types within a gene, not genes within a type.
  • Sample-level profiles with a gene–gene covariance. With Gaussian profiles and known moments, the posterior mean of each \boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot j,i} is a Wiener filter; it is derived in the Bayesian Wiener-filter vignette.

On the measurement side, these methods need the bulk on a linear scale (FPKM for CSNet). When the bulk is normalised by its own library size, the known weights act as RNA fractions \boldsymbol{q}_{\cdot i}, not as cell fractions (Sec. 1).

Type-level moments given known proportions

CSNet inverts the DeCovarT arrow (Su et al. 2024). DeCovarT takes (\boldsymbol{\mu},\{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j\}) as plug-in and returns \boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}. CSNet takes \{\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}\}_{i=1}^{N} as known (from CIBERSORT, MuSiC, or DeCovarT itself) and returns type-level means and a sparse correlation network. The generative identities are the same convolution as Eq. 17 and Eq. 18, written across a cohort rather than one sample:

\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}\mid\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}] = \sum_j p_{ji}\,\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j}, \qquad \operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}\mid\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}) = \sum_j p_{ji}^{2}\,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j. \tag{19}

No Gaussian law is required for the moments. Let P\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times J} have entries P_{ij}=p_{ji} and H\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times J} have entries H_{ij}=p_{ji}^{2}. Gene-wise ordinary least squares on the linear mean recovers

\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{g\cdot} = (P^{\top}P)^{-1}P^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}_{g\cdot}, \tag{20}

the bulk analogue of a reference average, now identified from compositional contrast across samples rather than from purified cells. Centred residuals z_{gi}=y_{gi}-\sum_j p_{ji}\hat{\mu}_{gj} then satisfy the pairwise identity z_{gi}z_{g'i}=\sum_j p_{ji}^{2}\Sigma_{gg',j}+\varepsilon_{gg'i}. Least squares of the Hadamard products on H estimates each covariance entry,

\hat{\Sigma}_{gg',j} = \bigl[(H^{\top}H)^{-1}H^{\top}(\boldsymbol{z}_{g\cdot}\odot\boldsymbol{z}_{g'\cdot})\bigr]_{j}. \tag{21}

CSNet converts \hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_j to a correlation \hat{R}_j and applies an element-wise SCAD threshold. That is a marginal co-expression graph, not a Gaussian Markov precision. The Gaussian convolution log-likelihood in \{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j\}, which is the natural DeCovarT loss for the same parameters, is neither convex nor biconvex in those matrices; pairwise least squares is how CSNet avoids that optimisation (Su et al. 2024).

A DeCovarT-native sequel would keep Eq. 20–Eq. 21 as the moment step and map \hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_j to a sparse precision \boldsymbol{\Omega}_j (network inference), run after \boldsymbol{p} has been estimated (Figure 13). A CSNet correlation graph is not a DeCovarT precision.

P and H must have full column rank, so \boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i} has to vary across the N bulks. One sample identifies \boldsymbol{p} given (\boldsymbol{\mu},\{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j\}); it does not identify J covariance matrices. Rare types with almost constant p_{ji} leave the corresponding column of H weak, which is why CSNet recovers abundant-type co-expression more easily than microglia-scale weights. The method is a moment estimator: modest errors in the supplied \boldsymbol{p} are averaged over N, whereas DeCovarT’s likelihood for a single column is concentrated in \boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}.

Errors in variables (Sec. 2.2): the reverse problem, with the composition known and the latent profiles’ moments as the target; moments only.

Sample-level profiles with a covariance across cell types

Unico (Chen et al. 2025) takes the proportions as given, estimated beforehand by a reference-based method, and estimates for each gene the moments of the latent sample-level profiles, then the profiles themselves (a samples \times genes \times types tensor). Its model (equations 3–6, p. 11), in our notation, makes no distributional assumption:

y_{gi}=\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}_{g\cdot,i}+e_{gi}, \qquad \mathbb{E}\,\boldsymbol{x}_{g\cdot,i}=\boldsymbol{\mu}_{g\cdot}, \quad \operatorname{Cov}\boldsymbol{x}_{g\cdot,i}=\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g, \qquad \mathbb{E}\,e_{gi}=0, \quad \operatorname{Var}e_{gi}=\tau_g^{2}, \tag{22}

so that \operatorname{Var}(y_{gi})=\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}+\tau_g^{2}.

  • Estimator. A generalised method of moments per gene (equations 9–12, pp. 13–14): one first-moment condition, y_{gi}-\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{g\cdot}, and one second-moment condition, (y_{gi}-\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{g\cdot})^{2}-\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}-\tau_g^{2}, per sample, combined with a diagonal weight matrix; that is iterated weighted least squares, with non-negative means, a small ridge on \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g and samples beyond two standard deviations dropped (p. 14).
  • Profiles. The conditional expectation under a Gaussian working law (Theorem 1, p. 12), \hat{\boldsymbol{x}}_{g\cdot,i}=\boldsymbol{\mu}_{g\cdot}+\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}(y_{gi}-\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{g\cdot})/(\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}+\tau_g^{2}), the gene-wise, J\times J analogue of DeCovarT’s Wiener filter; TCA is the case \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g=\mathbf{I}. Distribution-free asymptotic tests of covariate effects at the cell-type level are offered (Fig. 3b, p. 8).

Critical remarks. \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g is identified only from many bulk samples of varying composition, and the plugged-in proportions are treated as exact. The bulk variance \boldsymbol{p}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g\boldsymbol{p} is quadratic in \boldsymbol{p}, like DeCovarT’s: with \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g=\operatorname{diag}\{(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j)_{gg}\}_j it is the variance of gene g under DeCovarT. The off-diagonal of \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g is what DeCovarT drops by assuming independent types; the gene–gene couplings are what Unico drops (our remark).

Errors in variables (Sec. 2.2): the reverse problem again, with two-moment conditions solved by a generalised method of moments.

Bayesian reference-based deconvolution

Bayesian methods put priors on the purified profiles, on the proportions, or on both, and report posterior summaries. They split by target: sample-level profiles (Sec. 4.1) or proportions (Sec. 4.2). A latent-profile Bayesian version of DeCovarT is derived in the Bayesian Wiener-filter vignette.

Cell-type-specific profiles

bMIND estimates sample-level profiles for proportions estimated beforehand (by NNLS or Bisque) (Wang et al. 2020). For gene g and subject i,

y_{gi}=\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}_{g\cdot,i}+e_{gi}, \qquad \boldsymbol{x}_{g\cdot,i}\sim\mathcal{N}_J(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{g\cdot},\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g), \qquad e_{gi}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_g^{2}), \tag{23}

with \boldsymbol{\mu}_{g\cdot}\sim\mathcal{N}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{g\cdot},0.5\mathbf{I}), \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g\sim\mathrm{IW}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}_g,50) and a non-informative prior on \sigma_g^{2}; the hyperparameters come from single-cell or single-nucleus summary statistics. Sampling is by MCMC (MCMCglmm), gene by gene. Condition-specific means \boldsymbol{\mu}_g^{f} give tests of cell-type-specific differential expression. The authors note that the uncertainty of the estimated proportions is not propagated.

EPIC-unmix (Tang et al. 2025) keeps the bMIND model and adds a second, empirical-Bayes step: the prior is re-centred on the step-one posterior means and on their covariance across the target samples, with an increased number of degrees of freedom The target samples are therefore used twice. The bulk enters on the \log_2 scale, so the linear mixing of Eq. 23 is a mixing of logarithms, which is not the physical sum of cells (\log\sum_jp_jx_j\neq\sum_jp_j\log x_j).

BLADE estimates proportions and sample-level profiles jointly (Andrade Barbosa et al. 2021): y_{gi}=\sum_jp_{ji}x_{gj,i} plus a log-normal error, with x_{gj,i}\sim\mathrm{LN}(m_{gj},\lambda_{gj}^{-1}), a normal-gamma prior on (m_{gj},\lambda_{gj}) centred on the log-scale mean and variance of single-cell data, and \boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}\sim\mathrm{Dir}(\boldsymbol{\alpha}_1). The mixing is on the linear scale (TPM). Inference is collapsed variational, with hyperparameters chosen on a grid by likelihood. The model is diagonal: no covariance across genes or across types.

BEDwARS treats the reference itself as noisy (Ghaffari et al. 2023): y_{gi}=\sum_j\mu_{gj}p_{ji}+E_{gi}, \log\mu_{gj}\sim\log\mu^{r}_{gj}+\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_j^{2}\log\mu^{r}_{gj}), \boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}\sim\mathrm{Dir}(\alpha\boldsymbol{p}_0), with half-Cauchy hyperpriors and Metropolis–Hastings chains. The signature is cohort-level: there is no sample-level profile. As written, the prior variance \sigma_j^{2}\log\mu^{r}_{gj} is not positive for reference values at or below one RPKM (our remark).

BayesPrism places a multinomial likelihood on bulk counts with a patient-derived single-cell prior and infers proportions and sample-level profiles jointly (Chu et al. 2022). The multinomial is the Poisson measurement model conditioned on the library size (Sec. 1.1), so BayesPrism is the count-scale member of this family.

The contrast with DeCovarT is the dimension of the covariance. bMIND and EPIC-unmix model how cell types covary for one gene across subjects; DeCovarT models how genes covary within one cell type. A separable covariance \operatorname{Cov}(\operatorname{vec}\boldsymbol{X}_i)=\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\otimes\boldsymbol{\Sigma} for the G\times J matrix of purified profiles would contain both as special cases (our remark); no reviewed method fits it.

Proportions

DSection is the continuous, Gaussian route (Erkkilä et al. 2010): y_{gi}\sim\mathcal{N}\bigl(\sum_jp_{ji}x_{gjh(i)},\lambda_g^{-1}\bigr), with type profiles specific to the condition h(i) of sample i, x_{gjh}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_{gjh},\nu), \lambda_g\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(\alpha,\beta) and \boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}\sim\mathrm{Dir}(w_0\boldsymbol{p}_{0i}) centred on a prior guess of the proportions, which is needed for identifiability. Sampling is Gibbs for the profiles and the precision and Metropolis–Hastings with Dirichlet proposals for the proportions. The paper offers no log-normal option and recommends linear data. The variance depends on the gene but not on the proportions.

gnSPADE (Xie and Cui 2026) is the count route, and it is reference-free. Each UMI of spot i draws a label z\sim\mathrm{Mult}(\boldsymbol{q}_{\cdot i}) and then a gene from the profile of that label, so \boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}\mid\boldsymbol{q}_{\cdot i}\sim\mathrm{Mult}(L_i,\sum_jq_{ji}\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\cdot j}), with L_i the number of UMIs: latent Dirichlet allocation with a Markov random field over the labels built from a protein interaction network. Inference is collapsed Gibbs.

The two differ where the measurement model of Sec. 1 bites.

  • Variance. In gnSPADE the variance is fixed by the mean (the multinomial is a Poisson measurement conditioned on the total). In DSection it is a free gene-wise constant that does not grow with the mean, which a UMI measurement contradicts.
  • What the weights are. gnSPADE shares UMIs, so the label probabilities are transcript fractions \boldsymbol{q}_{\cdot i}; converting them to cell fractions needs S_j. DSection estimates whatever its reference scale encodes.
  • Profile variability. Neither model has a type-level variability of profiles across samples beyond the prior of DSection; neither has a gene–gene covariance. The gene network of gnSPADE acts on labels, not on expression.

Semi-reference deconvolution: one unknown component

Semi-reference methods have references for J-1 types and estimate an unknown component, usually tumour, together with the proportions. With one component unknown, the convolution of univariate laws has to be written explicitly, and its tractability drives the choice of law.

DeMix and DeMixT. DeMix mixes a tumour and one normal component; DeMixT adds a second normal component (Ahn et al. 2013; Wang et al. 2018):

y_{gi}=\pi_{1,i}N_{1,gi}+\pi_{2,i}N_{2,gi}+(1-\pi_{1,i}-\pi_{2,i})T_{gi}, \qquad N_{j,gi},T_{gi}\sim\log_2\text{-normal}. \tag{24}

The mixing is linear on the raw scale, and the density of a sum of log-normals has no closed form, so DeMixT integrates numerically (a double integral for three components). The normal-component parameters are plugged in from unmatched normal samples; the proportions and the tumour parameters are maximised by iterated conditional modes, gene and sample blocks in parallel. When the two normal means are close, the likelihood is flat in (\pi_1,\pi_2); a gene-set component-merging step first estimates the tumour proportion on genes where they agree. Genes are independent.

DeMixNB replaces the log-normal by a negative binomial for sparse counts (miRNA, spatial spots) (Montierth et al. 2025): T_{gi}\sim\mathrm{NB}(\pi_i\mu_{tg},\phi_{tg}), N_{gi}\sim\mathrm{NB}((1-\pi_i)\mu_{ng},\phi_{ng}) and y_{gi}=T_{gi}+N_{gi}, whose density is the finite sum \sum_{z=0}^{y}f_T(z)f_N(y-z). The proportions scale the means, not the dispersions. Read with Sec. 1, \mathrm{NB}(\pi\mu,\phi) is the binomial thinning of \mathrm{NB}(\mu,\phi): a Poisson measurement of a Gamma-distributed rate, with the rates mixed linearly (our remark). That makes DeMixNB the semi-reference model closest to a UMI measurement. Its \pi_i is a transcript fraction. The method is a preprint.

BayICE models \log(\text{count}+1) as Gaussian with mean \alpha_g+\sum_jw_{ji}\beta_{gj}+w_{0i}\beta_{g0}, a convex combination of type effects plus an unknown-class effect, with spike-and-slab priors on the type effects (marker selection with a Bayesian false discovery rate) and a Dirichlet prior on the weights (Tai et al. 2021). Inference is Gibbs with Metropolis–Hastings steps. The mixing is on the log scale, so it is a mean regression rather than a convolution, and the variances are gene-wise, not type-specific.

ISOpureR places a multinomial on the discretised tumour profile, with probability vector \alpha_i\boldsymbol{c}_i+\sum_r\omega_{ri}\boldsymbol{x}^{\mathrm{ref}}_r: the normal part is a convex combination of individual reference samples, the cancer profile \boldsymbol{c}_i is shrunk towards a cohort mean by a Dirichlet prior, and the estimate is a MAP by block coordinate descent (Anghel et al. 2015). Genes are coupled through the multinomial simplex; there is no overdispersion. Its \alpha_i is a fraction of transcripts.

Reference-free deconvolution with co-expression structure

Without a reference, deconvolution is a non-negative matrix factorisation \boldsymbol{Y}\approx\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{P} with the columns of \boldsymbol{P} on the simplex. Three recent methods add gene–gene structure to that factorisation, in three different ways.

DSSC (Wang et al. 2024) fits the bulk and, in addition, the Gram matrices of genes and of samples :

\min_{\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{P}\ge 0} \lVert\boldsymbol{Y}-\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{P}\rVert_F^{2} +\lambda_1\lVert\boldsymbol{K}_N-\boldsymbol{P}^{\top}\boldsymbol{P}\rVert_F^{2} +\lambda_2\lVert\boldsymbol{K}_G-\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\top}\rVert_F^{2} +\lambda_c\lVert\boldsymbol{\mu}-\mathcal{T}(\boldsymbol{Y}_{\mathrm{sc}})\rVert_F^{2}, \tag{25}

where \boldsymbol{K}_G and \boldsymbol{K}_N are similarity kernels 1/(1+d) built from Pearson distances of the same bulk, and the last term optionally pulls the signature towards a transform \mathcal{T} of a single-cell reference. Multiplicative updates are run without the sum-to-one constraint and the proportions are normalised afterwards. The gene term matches \boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\top} to a data similarity; expanded, it keeps the affinity part of a graph-Laplacian penalty and replaces its degree term by a quartic term, so it corresponds to no Gaussian Markov random field (our remark).

GSNMF+ (Li et al. 2025) regularises the rows of the signature with a kernel co-expression graph built on the bulk augmented by single-cell pseudo-bulks, and pulls marker rows towards the simplex vertices It states identifiability conditions (separability, or sufficiently scattered factors) and that the Frobenius loss is the Gaussian maximum-likelihood estimate. With a Euclidean distance its graph term would be \operatorname{tr}(\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\top}\boldsymbol{L}_G\boldsymbol{\mu}), the log-density of an intrinsic Gaussian Markov random field prior on the signature; with the cosine distance it uses, the term is quartic.

swCAM estimates sample-specific signatures (Chen et al. 2022). After convex analysis of mixtures has fixed \boldsymbol{\mu} and \boldsymbol{P}, it solves

\min_{\{\boldsymbol{\Delta}_i\}} \tfrac12\sum_i\lVert\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}-(\boldsymbol{\mu}+\boldsymbol{\Delta}_i)\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}\rVert_2^{2} +\lambda\sum_j\lVert\boldsymbol{T}_j\rVert_{*}, \tag{26}

where \boldsymbol{T}_j stacks the deviations of type j over samples and \lVert\cdot\rVert_* is the nuclear norm. The problem is convex for fixed \boldsymbol{\mu} and \boldsymbol{P} and is solved by ADMM. There is no co-expression graph. Because \lVert\boldsymbol{T}\rVert_*=\min_{\boldsymbol{U}\boldsymbol{V}^{\top}=\boldsymbol{T}}\tfrac12(\lVert\boldsymbol{U}\rVert_F^{2}+\lVert\boldsymbol{V}\rVert_F^{2}), the penalty is the MAP of a Gaussian factor model (Figure 17), which implies a low-rank gene–gene covariance within each type.

Three ways gene covariance enters deconvolution

  1. Graph regularisation of a factorisation. A co-expression graph smooths the signature (GSNMF+). Its probabilistic reading is a Gaussian Markov random field prior on the signature, exact only for a Euclidean, quadratic penalty.
  2. Similarity matching to the bulk itself. The Gram matrices of the factors are fitted to similarities computed from the same data (DSSC). The data are used twice, and no likelihood is implied.
  3. Covariance in a likelihood, a moment equation or a prior. The gene–gene covariance of each type enters the bulk law: as a plug-in in DeCovarT, as moment equations in DECALS and MEAD, as the estimand in CSNet, and implicitly as a low-rank factor structure in swCAM. bMIND and EPIC-unmix belong here with the transposed object, a covariance across cell types.

All three reference-free methods use a squared Frobenius loss, that is a homoscedastic Gaussian likelihood, and therefore ignore the mean–variance relationship of counts (Sec. 1.1).

Synthesis

Caveats and defaults

  1. Scale. Mixing is additive only on a linear scale. Methods that mix logarithms (BayICE, EPIC-unmix) estimate weights of a different, non-physical sum.
  2. Cell versus RNA fractions. Count and topic models (ISOpureR, gnSPADE, DeMixNB, BayesPrism) and any fit on library-normalised bulk return transcript fractions; cell fractions need the cell sizes S_j (RNA-to-cell conversion).
  3. Mean–variance relationship. A constant residual variance (DSection, BEDwARS, NMF with a Frobenius loss) contradicts the Poisson measurement of UMI counts, whose variance grows with the mean. Count likelihoods or explicit variance functions respect it (GLM view).
  4. Linear or quadratic weights. Independent cells give a variance linear in the proportions (RNA-Sieve, ReDeconv); a random population profile gives a quadratic weight (MuSiC, DECALS, CSNet, DeCovarT). Single-cell references with one donor identify only the first (single-cell generative vignette).
  5. Which covariance. G\times G within a type (DeCovarT, DECALS, CSNet) and J\times J within a gene (bMIND, EPIC-unmix, Unico) answer different questions; neither family fits both.
  6. Data reuse. Empirical-Bayes re-centring on the target samples (EPIC-unmix), similarity graphs built from the bulk being factorised (DSSC, GSNMF+) and priors built from the same single-cell source as the benchmark bulk (BLADE group mode) inflate apparent accuracy.
  7. Propagated uncertainty. Weighted moment estimators (MuSiC, DWLS, deMixSC) return point estimates only (Sec. 2.2). Few methods propagate the uncertainty of the reference (RNA-Sieve, MEAD, DeCovarT’s reference bootstrap) or of the proportions into downstream profiles (bMIND and Unico do not).
  8. Identifiability. Gene-wise scales with perfect markers (MEAD), collinear reference means (DeMixT), and reference-free factorisations without separability (GSNMF+) all leave the proportions unidentified, whatever the sample size.

Methods to add to this review

Already in the bibliography and worth a section: BLEND, probabilistic deconvolution with automated reference selection (Huang et al. 2024); DeconV, a Poisson model aggregated from single cells (Gynter et al. 2023); Imply, personalised reference profiles (Meng et al. 2024); and DecOT, an optimal transport loss (Liu et al. 2022). CIBERSORTx (Newman et al. 2019) extends the signature approach to high-resolution, sample-level profiles.
